mentions.excerpt: In late May, Apollo was raising $38 billion of debt to put Google’s TPUs, not Nvidia’s GPUs, behind Anthropic.
Ten weeks later, Apollo and Blackstone were assembling a $35 billion first tranche of an “AI XPU platform”: twenty gigawatts of Broadcom-designed compute through 2028.
Apollo and Blackstone can assemble capital for an AI XPU platform without asking any single balance sheet to carry the full future.
Big Tech now spends more each year on AI than the United States spent on the Apollo program after inflation.
Michael Burry, citing Apollo’s Torsten Slok, says private non-residential construction excluding data centers fell 7.9% year over year in June.

Apollo, relayed by DeepValue Capital, assumes hyperscaler operating cash flow triples from $600 billion to $2 trillion, with OpenAI and Anthropic accounting for more than half of a $2.3 trillion backlog.
Torsten Slok, Apollo’s chief economist, turns the revenue question into an accounting test.
Apollo’s analysis makes the mismatch difficult to wave away.
Apollo’s credit analysis captures a debt price dependent on a large improvement.
Apollo put the question plainly; the checkout supplies the cash.
Torsten Slok of Apollo says adding technology analysts’ forecasts roughly doubles the sector’s operating cash flow to about $2.4 trillion by 2028, a gain of more than $1.2 trillion.
Leyla Kunimoto, citing an Apollo presentation, reports that hyperscalers sold close to $250 billion of high-grade bonds in 2026, more than in the previous ten years combined.

sides.claim: Consensus expects hyperscalers' operating cash flow to more than triple by 2030, outpacing the sharp increase in AI-driven capex, based on FactSet and Apollo Chief Economist sources for Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Oracle.
